title: The First Magic Angle Beyond the Chiral Limit in Twisted Bilayer Graphene
authors: Leonardo A. Navarro-Labastida, Pierre A. Pantaleon, Francisco Guinea, Gerardo G. Naumis
abstract: We develop a squared-Hamiltonian description of twisted bilayer graphene beyond the chiral limit to explain why the first magic angle remains robust under lattice relaxation, while higher-order magic angles are strongly destabilized. Starting from the non-chiral Bistritzer--MacDonald model with finite same-sublattice tunneling, we show that lattice relaxation reshapes the effective confinement landscape rather than acting as a simple perturbation of the chiral theory. A central result is that the realistic relaxation-renormalized tunneling ratio lies close to a special confinement point where the oscillatory part of the symmetric confinement potential nearly cancels. This places realistic twisted bilayer graphene near a nearly uniform confinement regime. At the same time, finite same-sublattice tunneling activates an additional inter-sublattice current-like channel that competes with the chiral orbital channel. The first magic angle survives because these confinement and current-like contributions remain balanced, whereas higher-order magic angles lose this balance through stronger remote-band hybridization and enhanced real-space localization around AA regions. Our results provide a single-particle mechanism for the breakdown of the chiral magic-angle hierarchy and clarify why the experimentally relevant first magic angle remains the most stable remnant of the chiral flat-band structure.
summary: This work develops a theoretical model for twisted bilayer graphene, moving beyond the idealized chiral limit to include effects from lattice relaxation. It shows that the first magic angle is uniquely stable because the competing effects of confinement and current-like channels balance out, providing a single-particle mechanism for the breakdown of the magic-angle hierarchy.
main_problem: The paper aims to explain the physical mechanism behind the differential stability of magic angles in twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) when lattice relaxation is considered.
main_result: The first magic angle remains robust because the effects of lattice relaxation (confinement and current-like channels) remain balanced, whereas higher-order angles lose this balance due to enhanced hybridization and localization.
method: The analysis uses a single-particle, continuum model Hamiltonian, employing a squared-Hamiltonian description and perturbative expansion to analyze deviations from the ideal chiral limit.
model_or_system: The system is Twisted Bilayer Graphene (TBG) modeled by a non-chiral Bistritzer–MacDonald Hamiltonian. The model incorporates the effect of lattice relaxation via a finite same-sublattice tunneling term, parameterized by $\kappa = w_{AA}/w_{AB}$.
key_observables: Electronic bandwidth suppression (flat bands), spectral squeezing, and the energy shift ($\Delta E$) as a function of the twist angle ($\alpha$).
important_parameters: The tunneling ratio $\kappa$ (deviation from the chiral limit, $\kappa=0$), and the twist-angle coupling $\alpha$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on a single-valley continuum theory and uses perturbative methods, which are assumed valid only for small twist angles ($\alpha$).
figures_summary: Figures compare band structures and electronic densities between the ideal chiral limit ($\kappa=0$) and the realistic non-chiral case ($\kappa=0.7$), showing spectral differences and enhanced localization for finite $\kappa$.
paper_structure:
The paper develops the squared-Hamiltonian formalism, analyzes the effect of finite same-sublattice tunneling ($\kappa 
eq 0$) perturbatively, and compares the resulting electronic structure to the known chiral limit results to deduce the stability mechanism.
why_interesting:
While focused on condensed matter, the concept of symmetry protection (chiral limit) breaking by realistic perturbations ($\kappa 
eq 0$) and the resulting stability hierarchy is relevant to understanding topological phases in open quantum systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Band structure for the first magic angle, panels (a) and (b), and for a higher-order magic angle, panels (c) and (d), comparing the chiral model with the relaxation-renormalized non-chiral model at κ = 0.7. In the chiral model, the bands squeeze as a function of α, and the gap decreases exponentially as predicted by the chiral scaling theory. In the non-chiral model, the hybridization between the central bands and the first remote bands becomes substantially stronger, especially at small twist angles where the gap tends to close systematically.

FIG. 2. E2(α) at the Γ point in semi-logarithmic scale for the non-chiral model κ ≈0.7 (red curve), compared with the chiral model κ = 0 (blue curve). The vertical black lines indicate the magic angles of the chiral theory. While the chiral model preserves an exponential squeezing of the spectrum, finite κ partially blocks this behavior and produces substantial deviations at higher-order magic angles.

FIG. 3. Electronic density at the Γ point. First magic angle α1 = 0.586 for (a) the chiral limit κ = 0 and (b) the non-chiral model with κ = 0.7. Electronic density for the higher-order magic angle α9 = 12.860 for (c) the chiral limit κ = 0 and (d) the non-chiral model κ = 0.7. Finite κ induces a pronounced localization of the electronic density around the AA stacking regions.

FIG. 4. Fourier coefficients |am,n|2 for the chiral (left column) and non-chiral (right column) models. Results are shown for the first magic angle, α1 = 0.586, and for the higher-order magic angle, α9 = 12.860. The non-chiral calculations use κ = 0.7, following previous estimates for relaxation-renormalized TBG [57]. Finite κ shifts spectral weight toward larger |Kmn|, indicating stronger localization in real space. It also enhances the trigonal anisotropy of the Fourier distribution while preserving the underlying C3 symmetry.

FIG. 5. Effective potentials of the non-chiral squared Hamiltonian in real space. Panels (a) and (b) show the real and imaginary components of the intrinsic pseudo-magnetic vector potential A(r), respectively. Panels (c) and (d) display the antisymmetric confinement potential ∆(r) = i[Ax, Ay] and the symmetric confinement term A2(r). The non-chiral nature of the model introduces the complex sublattice-sector coupling potential VS(r), whose modulus and phase are shown in panels (e) and (f), respectively.
